title: The Complete Guide to Modern Institutional ID Card Security
seoTitle: Modern ID Card Security: PVC, Printing and RFID Guide
subtitle: What actually makes a school, college or office ID card hard to fake: the card body, the print, the chip and, just as important, the process around it.
excerpt: A practical guide to ID card security for schools, colleges and offices: card body, print and lamination, visual deterrents, RFID chip choice and the data and replacement process behind the card.
alt: Institutional security PVC ID cards and RFID contactless credentials

tableOfContents.title: 1. Start with the card body, not the chip
3. Choosing an RFID chip that is hard to clone
5. A one-page checklist before you order
6. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

keyTakeaways: The ID-1 format (also sold as CR80) is 85.60 mm x 53.98 mm with a nominal thickness of 0.76 mm; a card that is noticeably thinner or flimsier is a warning sign.
Most security failures are process failures: no photo check, no lost-card routine, no expiry. Fix these before buying a more expensive chip.
Cheap 125 kHz proximity cards broadcast a fixed number that inexpensive copiers can duplicate; MIFARE Classic's cipher was publicly broken in 2008. If a gate matters, ask for a newer chip family.
Ask every supplier to show a sample, a proof and what happens to your student or staff data.

content.lead: An ID card is a small object with a big job. It tells a guard, a librarian or a lab technician that the person in front of them belongs there. When that fails, it usually fails in an ordinary way: a card that peels at the corners, a photo that no one compares to the face, a gate that opens for a copied card, or a lost card that stays active for a year. This guide walks through the layers that matter, in the order we think they matter, using public standards and published research rather than marketing claims.

sections.heading: 1. Start with the card body, not the chip
body: Most institutional cards worldwide follow the ID-1 format defined in ISO/IEC 7810, often called CR80 in the printing trade. The format is 85.60 mm by 53.98 mm with rounded corners and a nominal thickness of 0.76 mm, which is about 30 mil. The standard allows a tolerance on thickness, so two genuine cards can differ slightly, but a card that bends easily or measures clearly thinner is not the same product.

Why does this matter for security? Because the card body is what carries every other feature. A rigid PVC core holds a printed image and a chip inlay in a stable position. A paper card sealed in a pouch does not: moisture and skin oils get in at the cut edges, the print clouds, and the layers can be separated and re-assembled with a different photo. A solid card cannot be altered that way without leaving visible damage.

For schools and colleges, durability is also a security feature in a quieter sense. A card that is still readable and still looks like the original at the end of the year is a card a guard can trust. A card that has gone soft and faded invites a quick glance and a nod.

tipBox.title: Quick physical test
tipBox.text: Hold a sample card by one corner and flex it gently. It should spring back, the print should not crack, and the edges should be clean with no visible glue line. Ask your supplier for the same sample you will receive, not a showpiece.

sections.heading: 2. Print, lamination and visual checks
body: Print quality is the second layer. Photo ID cards are normally printed with a thermal process, either direct to card or retransfer, and finished with a protective overlay. The practical differences for a buyer are sharpness of the photo, whether colour runs to the very edge of the card, and how the surface wears. Ask for a printed sample of your own design rather than a stock image, because a logo with fine lines or a dark photo background tests the printer far more than a plain sample.

Visual deterrents such as micro-text, guilloche-style patterns, holographic overlays or a ghost image of the photo make counterfeiting harder because they are difficult to reproduce on an office printer. They do not stop a determined forger, and they only help if the person checking the card knows what to look for. If you add one, tell the guards and front-desk staff what it is and what a genuine card looks like.

A simpler, often more effective step is consistent design. Use one layout for students, a different colour band for staff, another for visitors, and a different year colour for each batch. A guard can then spot a wrong colour or an expired year from several steps away.

sections.heading: 3. Choosing an RFID chip that is hard to clone
body: If your card opens doors, marks attendance or pays for meals, the chip matters. Three families come up in most Indian campuses and offices.

Low-frequency 125 kHz proximity cards, such as EM4100 or HID Prox, simply transmit a fixed number. Security testing by the industry press found that most 125 kHz formats are not encrypted at all and that a copier costing about $30 produced working duplicates; another vendor reported that copying takes no more than about 15 seconds. They are fine for low-risk uses such as a canteen or an attendance machine, but they should not be the only thing protecting a hostel or a lab.

MIFARE Classic, a 13.56 MHz card that is still widely deployed, uses a proprietary cipher called Crypto1. Researchers at Radboud University reconstructed the cipher and cloned a card in 2008, and later work showed that knowing one key could reveal the others. NXP's own security statement recommends moving to newer products such as MIFARE Plus or DESFire where security matters, and says countermeasures for Classic only partly help unless every card has its own keys. This does not mean old Classic systems are useless, but it does mean you should not choose Classic for a new project that guards something valuable.

Newer 13.56 MHz families that use mutual authentication make copying far harder. The right choice for you depends on your reader and software, which is why the first question to ask any supplier is which chips your existing readers support. IDGen can supply RFID cards matched to the reader you use; send us the reader model before ordering and we will confirm compatibility.

tipBox.title: Do not guess the chip
tipBox.text: Ask your access-control vendor for the exact card type and data format the reader expects. A wrong frequency means cards that never register, and a wrong format means numbers that do not match your database.

sections.heading: 4. The process around the card
body: Strong cards fail when the process is weak. Four habits cost almost nothing and close most of the gaps.

Check the photo against the person at issue time, not later. A card that was issued with the wrong photo is a perfectly genuine card for the wrong person. Keep the master data in one place, with one spelling per name, and print from that record.

Have a lost-card routine. The student or staff member reports the loss, the old card is deactivated at the gate or in the database, and the new card carries a visible mark such as a reissue date. Without that, a lost card is a free key.
Set an expiry. A card with the academic year on it, or a colour that changes every year, makes old cards obvious. Collect cards from leavers.

Handle the data carefully. Names, photos and ID numbers are personal data. In India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its rules govern how personal data is handled, and the rules were notified in November 2025 with provisions phasing in over about eighteen months. Educational institutions have specific provisions, so check the current text or ask your legal adviser what applies to you. Whatever the law requires, the sensible baseline is to share student data only with the people who need it, and only for the purpose of making the card.

sections.heading: 5. A one-page checklist before you order
body: Before you ask for a quote, write down answers to these questions. They make the quotation faster and the cards better.
• What is the card for: identification only, or also gate access, attendance, library or payments?
• What does the reader or software expect: frequency, chip family, output format?
• How many cards now, and how many will you add during the year?
• What colours or layout will separate students, staff and visitors?
• Who will check photos, and who will approve the proof?
• How will lost and expired cards be handled?

At IDGen, an order is produced at our facility in Guwahati and dispatched within 72 hours of approval, with a proof sent first so the design and data are checked before printing. Ask for a physical sample if you are planning a large batch.

sections.heading: 6. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
body: These are the mistakes we see most often.
• Buying the chip before fixing the process: an expensive card issued with an unchecked photo is still the wrong card in the right hands.
• Using the same card design for every group, so a visitor card looks like a staff card.
• Never retiring old cards. A card that never expires is a permanent key.
• Choosing a chip family because it is cheap, then discovering the reader needs a different one.
• Skipping the sample, and learning about colour, thickness or finish only when the whole batch arrives.

sections.heading: 7. Frequently asked questions
body: Is a thicker card always more secure? No. Thickness makes the card durable, but security comes from the layers around it: print, finish, chip and process. A standard ID-1 card at about 0.76 mm is the normal, and expected, thickness.
Do we need holograms? Only if you will train the people checking cards to look for them. A consistent design with colour bands and expiry marks is more useful for most schools.
Is 125 kHz acceptable for a school? For low-risk uses such as a canteen or a simple attendance punch, yes. For hostel, lab or exam-hall access, ask for a newer 13.56 MHz family.
What if we already use MIFARE Classic? Existing systems do not need to be replaced overnight, but plan a migration, and avoid choosing Classic for new projects that guard valuable areas.
How should we handle lost cards? Report, deactivate, reissue with a visible mark, and keep a log. The deactivation step is the one most often missed.

title: Why Ultrasonic Sealing Is Used for Institutional Lanyards
seoTitle: Ultrasonic Lanyard Sealing: How It Works and When to Use It
subtitle: A plain explanation of ultrasonic welding for lanyards and cards, what it does better than stitching, where it does not help, and what to ask a supplier.
excerpt: How ultrasonic welding joins lanyard ends and seals cards, the materials it works on, its limits, and what buyers should check before ordering.
alt: Ultrasonic welded custom printed satin lanyards

tableOfContents.title: 2. Welded joints compared with stitched joints
4. Choosing the rest of the lanyard
5. What to ask before you order
6. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

keyTakeaways: Ultrasonic welding joins materials with high-frequency vibration and pressure, without glue or thread; heat is generated mainly at the joint.
It works best on thermoplastic (synthetic) fabrics, so it suits polyester lanyards and is a poor fit for cotton or other natural fibres.
A welded end avoids exposed thread that can unravel, but the weld still needs checking: ask for a sample and pull-test it.
Width, material, attachment and breakaway choice matter as much as the join.

content.lead: A lanyard is the cheapest part of an ID setup and the part most likely to fail. The hook comes loose, the stitching frays, the end curls, or the printing rubs off. Ultrasonic welding is one way of making the join without thread, and it is worth understanding what it does and does not do before you pay extra for it.

sections.heading: 1. How ultrasonic welding works
body: In ultrasonic welding, the parts to be joined are pressed between a fixed shaped surface, the anvil, and a vibrating tool called a sonotrode or horn. The horn is driven by a transducer and vibrates at a frequency above the range of human hearing, commonly around 20 to 40 kHz for textiles. The vibration turns into heat and pressure right where the two layers meet, softens the material and fuses it as it cools. Because the heat is produced mainly at the join, the rest of the lanyard does not need to be heated.
No adhesive, thread or rivet is involved. That is the practical attraction for lanyards: the join is part of the ribbon rather than something added to it.

sections.heading: 2. Welded joints compared with stitched joints
body: A stitched end has two weaknesses. The thread can wear through where it rubs against clothing, and a cut edge can fray if it is not sealed. A welded end seals the edge as part of the same step, which leaves a neat, flat finish with no loose thread to catch or unravel.

That is a real advantage on lanyards worn all day by students or factory staff. It does not mean a welded join is unbreakable. The strength of a weld depends on the material, the thickness, the pressure and the settings used, so it should be checked on a sample rather than assumed.

Welded finishes also tend to look cleaner on printed ribbons, because there is no bulky seam to interrupt the print. For schools that want a tidy, uniform look across hundreds of lanyards, that consistency is useful.

sections.heading: 3. What it cannot do
body: Ultrasonic welding needs thermoplastic material that melts and fuses under heat. Polyester and nylon ribbons qualify. Cotton and other natural fibres do not weld well on their own and generally need an adhesive film or a different join.
Thickness is another limit. Very thick or multi-layer material can overheat on the outside before the inside softens, so the process suits flat ribbon better than bulky trim.
Finally, welding does nothing for the parts that fail most often in practice: the hook, the clip and the card holder. A perfect weld on a weak hook still leaves you with a lost card.

tipBox.title: Test before you commit
tipBox.text: Ask for two sample lanyards. Pull the welded end hard, flex it twenty times and rub the printed side with a damp cloth. A good sample passes without loosening, cracking or colour transfer.

sections.heading: 4. Choosing the rest of the lanyard
body: Width. Many institutions choose 20 mm for adults and a narrower width for younger children, because a wide ribbon on a small child is uncomfortable. Whatever you choose, match it to the lanyard slot of your holder.

Material and print. Sublimation printing, where dye is transferred into polyester fibres, gives full-colour designs that do not sit on top of the ribbon and therefore resist rubbing better than printed ink. It needs polyester, which is also the material that welds well, so the two choices go together.

Attachment. Fish hooks, swivel hooks, clips and breakaway connectors each suit different uses. Breakaway connectors release under a strong pull, which is a sensible safeguard in labs, workshops, hostels and play areas.
Holders. A rigid holder takes the strain that would otherwise tear the punched hole in the card. Our blog on V-1, V-2 and H-1 holders explains the choices.

sections.heading: 5. What to ask before you order
body: Ask the supplier which fabric the lanyard is made of and how the ends are finished. Ask for a sample of the exact width, print and hook you are buying. Ask what the breakaway releases at and whether it can be replaced. Ask how many days the order takes and how it will reach you.

IDGen offers ultrasonic sealing on cards and lanyards as part of its institutional setups, and orders are dispatched from our Guwahati facility within 72 hours of approval, shipping by courier. If you are unsure which combination suits your students or staff, tell us who will wear it and where, and we will suggest one.

sections.heading: 6. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
body: These are the mistakes we see most often.
• Assuming a welded end is stronger than the hook. The hook is usually the weaker part.
• Choosing cotton or natural-fibre ribbon and expecting a welded finish.
• Ordering a wide ribbon for small children because it looks good in the sample.
• Skipping the pull test on a sample lanyard.
• Forgetting that a printed side faces outward: check where the join sits relative to the print.

sections.heading: 7. Frequently asked questions
body: Is ultrasonic welding the same as heat sealing? Both melt the material, but ultrasonic welding generates heat at the join through vibration, so the surrounding area stays cooler.
Can any lanyard be welded? No. It suits thermoplastic fabrics such as polyester and nylon, and works best on flat ribbon.
Does welding make the lanyard waterproof? No. It seals the join; it does not change the ribbon.
What width should we choose? 20 mm is common for adults. For small children, choose a narrower ribbon and a breakaway connector.
Do cards also get ultrasonically sealed? IDGen offers ultrasonic sealing on cards as an option for a tamper-evident, long-life finish; ask for a sample to see the look.

title: V-1 vs V-2 vs H-1: Choosing the Right Card Holder for Your Team
seoTitle: V-1, V-2 and H-1 Card Holders: How to Choose
subtitle: A practical guide to portrait, landscape and four-side-lock holders, with guidance on who should get which and what it costs per piece.
excerpt: Compare IDGen's V-1, H-1 and V-2 card holders, plus the crystal acrylic option, and learn how to match holder, card layout and lanyard slot.
alt: Polycarbonate rigid ID card holders V-1, V-2, H-1 models

tableOfContents.title: 1. Why a card needs a holder
2. Match the holder to the card layout
5. Fit, slot and lanyard checks before you order
6. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

keyTakeaways: A holder takes the load that a punched hole would otherwise put on the card, so it extends card life and protects an RFID antenna.
Choose orientation first: vertical or horizontal depends on how your card is designed, not on taste.
V-2's four-side lock suits people who bend, climb or run; V-1 and H-1 suit people who show the card often.
Check the lanyard slot width against your lanyard before you order.

content.lead: Teams spend days on the card design and minutes on the holder, and then spend the year replacing lost and cracked cards. The holder decides how a card hangs, how easily it comes out, and how long the card lasts. This guide explains the three standard holders IDGen supplies and how to choose between them.

sections.heading: 1. Why a card needs a holder
body: A CR80 PVC card is tough, but a hole punched through it is a weak point. Every movement of the lanyard pulls on that edge, and over months small cracks spread from the hole until the top of the card gives way. For cards with an RFID chip, a punched slot also risks cutting close to the antenna loop.

A rigid holder moves that load onto a moulded polycarbonate shell. The card stays flat, the corners are shielded from knocks, and the card can be replaced without replacing the lanyard. For most institutions that is the cheapest way to cut reprints.

sections.heading: 2. Match the holder to the card layout
body: Start with the card. Student cards are usually vertical, with the photo at the top and the details below. Many corporate cards are horizontal, especially where there is a wide logo, a long title or a second language. Pick the holder that matches your card layout; turning a card sideways in a holder meant for the other orientation puts the text on its side.

Also think about what the card shows from a distance. A vertical card shows the photo and name more prominently. A horizontal card shows a wide logo and designation better. If people mostly need to see a name across a table, vertical is usually better; if the card is checked at a reception counter, horizontal works well.

sections.heading: 3. The three standard models
body: Model V-1 (₹6 per piece). A portrait drop-in holder for vertical CR80 cards, 86 x 54 mm. It has an open top slip-in slot and a contoured thumb groove at the bottom for quick removal. It suits students, school staff, desks and any place where the card is taken out often, for example to be checked or swiped.

Model H-1 (₹6 per piece). A landscape holder with a centred 20 mm lanyard slot and side chain holes, so the card hangs level on the chest. It suits corporate cards with wide layouts, dual logos or long job titles.

Model V-2 (₹7 per piece). A four-side lock holder. Four snap-fit clips grip all edges of the card, so it does not slide out when the wearer bends, runs or climbs. It suits field staff, factory and warehouse teams, nurses, technicians and event security.
For VIP delegates and directors there is also the CV-1 crystal acrylic bevelled case at ₹25 per piece.

tipBox.title: Pro recommendation
tipBox.text: Specify V-2 for sports departments, plant and workshop staff, and event security, where a dropped or lost card causes real trouble.

sections.heading: 4. Who should get which
body: • Students and school staff: V-1 (vertical, ₹6)
• Corporate and horizontal card formats: H-1 (horizontal, ₹6)
• Field staff, hospital nurses, technicians: V-2 (four-side lock, ₹7)
• Directors and VIP delegates: CV-1 crystal acrylic case (₹25)
Prices are per piece and can change with quantity, so check the pricing page or ask for a quote on your order size.

If one organisation has several groups, it is normal to use two holder models. A school might give V-1 to students and V-2 to the sports staff. Colour-matched lanyards help each group stay recognisable.

sections.heading: 5. Fit, slot and lanyard checks before you order
body: • Card size: confirm your card is standard CR80 (about 85.6 x 54 mm).
• Orientation: confirm the holder matches the layout of your card.
• Lanyard slot: compare the slot width with the width of your lanyard; a 20 mm ribbon needs a slot that accepts it without folding.
• Hook: decide the hook type and make sure it can attach to the holder you chose.
• Sample: ask for a holder with a card in it and a lanyard on it, and wear it for a day.
IDGen supplies holders together with cards and lanyards so the set arrives matched. Orders are dispatched from our Guwahati facility within 72 hours of approval and shipped by courier.

sections.heading: 6. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
body: These are the mistakes we see most often.
• Ordering holders by price without checking the card orientation.
• Choosing a lanyard wider than the holder slot, so it folds and twists.
• Giving everyone the same holder when one group, such as sports or workshop staff, needs a lock.
• Ordering no spares for new admissions and joiners.
• Skipping a wear test: wear the sample for a day before approving.

sections.heading: 7. Frequently asked questions
body: Can a vertical card go in a horizontal holder? Physically it may fit, but the text will be sideways. Match holder and card layout.
Is V-2 worth the extra rupee? For people who bend, run or climb, yes. For students at desks, V-1 is usually enough.
Do holders protect RFID cards? They protect the card body and the corners from knocks and from the pull of the lanyard, which helps the antenna inside the card.
Can we get colour-matched holders? Ask for what is available for your quantity; colour options and prices are confirmed in the quote.
Do prices change with quantity? Yes, quantity affects pricing. Check the pricing page or request a quote.

title: RFID ID Cards Explained: 125 kHz vs 13.56 MHz and How to Choose
seoTitle: 125 kHz vs 13.56 MHz RFID Cards: How to Choose
subtitle: What the two common RFID card families actually are, how secure each one is, and the questions to ask your software team before any order.
excerpt: A buyer's guide to RFID ID cards: how they work, 125 kHz proximity vs 13.56 MHz cards, MIFARE and NFC, security differences, and a checklist to avoid ordering the wrong chip.
alt: Contactless RFID smart cards 13.56MHz and 125kHz coil inlays

tableOfContents.title: 3. 13.56 MHz cards: MIFARE, NFC and others
6. The checklist to send your software team
7. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

keyTakeaways: Contactless cards have no battery; the reader's field powers the chip, which answers with its data.
125 kHz proximity cards usually send a fixed number with no encryption and can be copied quickly with cheap equipment.
13.56 MHz cards include MIFARE and NFC chips and follow ISO/IEC 14443; their security varies a lot by family. MIFARE Classic's cipher was publicly broken in 2008.
The reader decides the chip. Get the reader model, chip family and data format in writing before you order.

content.lead: Attendance machines, hostel gates, library turnstiles and canteen counters all use RFID cards, and they do not all use the same kind. Order the wrong type and the cards simply will not be read, which usually becomes obvious only after the whole batch has been printed. This guide explains the families in plain terms and gives you a checklist to avoid that mistake.

sections.heading: 1. How a contactless card works
body: A contactless card contains a small chip connected to a coil antenna inside the plastic. It has no battery. When the card enters the reader's radio field, the antenna picks up energy, powers the chip, and the chip answers with its stored data. The reader passes that data to a controller or software, which decides whether to open the door, mark attendance or deduct a balance.
Two numbers describe the system: the frequency the reader uses, and the protocol and data format the chip and reader agree on. Both must match for the card to work.

sections.heading: 2. 125 kHz proximity cards
body: Low-frequency cards, commonly EM4100 and similar chips or the HID Prox format, work at 125 kHz. The read range is short, a few centimetres for a card held near the reader. They are simple, cheap and still common in older attendance machines and gates.

Most 125 kHz formats send a fixed identification number with no encryption and no authentication. That makes them easy to read and easy to copy. IPVM tested a copier costing about $30 that produced duplicates of popular HID Prox, ISOProx, EM4100 and AWID cards, and another vendor reported that the whole copy takes under about 15 seconds.
For a canteen, a punching machine or a low-value gate, that risk may be acceptable. For anything valuable, it is a poor choice.

sections.heading: 3. 13.56 MHz cards: MIFARE, NFC and others
body: The high-frequency family works at 13.56 MHz, and most cards in it follow the ISO/IEC 14443 standard. It includes MIFARE chips, many NFC tags such as NTAG, DESFire and others. These chips can store data in memory sectors and can use encryption, which is why they are used for library, transport and cashless systems as well as doors.

NFC is a subset: NFC-capable phones can read some 13.56 MHz tags, which is useful if you want a card or sticker that opens a web page or a verification link. It does not mean every 13.56 MHz card can be read by every phone.
Inside the family, security differs a great deal, as the next section shows.

sections.heading: 4. Security: what the research says
body: MIFARE Classic, a 13.56 MHz card sold in very large numbers, uses a proprietary cipher called Crypto1. In 2008, researchers at Radboud University reconstructed the cipher and showed that a card could be cloned without expensive equipment. In late 2014, NXP was notified of a newer card-only attack where knowing one key lets an attacker derive the others, and its security statement recommends moving to MIFARE Plus or DESFire, noting that countermeasures only help partly unless all keys are diversified. A 2024 research paper described a further attack against the card.

The practical lesson: a 13.56 MHz sticker on a card is not a guarantee of security. Ask which chip family and which security mode your project needs. Newer families that use mutual authentication make copying much harder than the old ones.

Security also depends on how the system is used. If the access system only checks the card's printed serial number, a strong chip adds little. If it checks encrypted data with unique keys, the chip's security counts.

sections.heading: 5. How to choose
body: • Low-risk, low-cost uses, such as a canteen or a simple punching machine, and an existing 125 kHz reader: a 125 kHz card is fine.
• New projects with access control or payments: choose a modern 13.56 MHz family with proper security, and check what the reader supports.

• Mixed old and new readers: some institutions need cards that work on both. Dual-frequency cards exist; ask whether the combination you need can be supplied and test a sample before ordering a large batch.
• Phone interaction: if you want phones to read the card, specify NFC-compatible chips.

tipBox.title: The reader decides
tipBox.text: Do not choose a chip because a brochure says it is secure. Choose the chip your reader accepts, then choose the most secure option within that. If you are buying new readers, choose them first.

sections.heading: 6. The checklist to send your software team
body: Confirm these five points in writing before you order:
1. Operating frequency: 125 kHz or 13.56 MHz?
2. Chip family: for example EM4100, MIFARE Classic, MIFARE Plus, DESFire, NTAG?
3. Output format: raw chip UID, 26-bit or 34-bit Wiegand, or another format?
4. Printing: do you want a number printed or laser-engraved on the card that matches the chip?
5. Test: ask for a small sample batch and try it on your own reader before the full order.
IDGen supplies RFID cards matched to the reader you use. Send us the reader model and we will confirm compatibility before printing.

sections.heading: 7. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
body: These are the mistakes we see most often.
• Choosing a card by frequency alone and ignoring the chip family and data format.
• Ordering the full batch before testing a sample on the real reader.
• Assuming every 13.56 MHz card is secure.
• Forgetting that the printed number on the card and the chip number are different things.
• Buying readers after the cards, and discovering they do not agree.

sections.heading: 8. Frequently asked questions
body: Can one card carry two frequencies? Dual-frequency cards exist. Ask whether the exact combination you need can be supplied and test a sample on both readers.
Will an NFC phone read my card? Only some 13.56 MHz chips, such as NFC tags, can be read by phones. Specify NFC-compatible chips if that matters.
What is a UID? A unique identifier stored in the chip. Some systems read only the UID; others read protected data.
Is 125 kHz obsolete? It is old, simple and still common, but it is not suited to high-value access control.
What do we send you to confirm compatibility? The reader or software name and model, the chip family it expects and the data format it reads.

title: Collecting Student Photos and Data Without the Chaos: A Practical Guide
seoTitle: Collecting Student ID Card Photos and Data: A Practical Guide
subtitle: Why photo and data collection causes most ID card delays, how to run it properly with or without software, and what changes under India's data protection law.
excerpt: A practical guide to collecting student photos and details for ID cards: common failures, a clean spreadsheet and photo format, an online collection workflow with IDGen Studio, and data protection basics.
alt: IDGen Studio digital student photo collection and proof approval portal

tableOfContents.title: 1. Where ID card orders actually get stuck
2. The spreadsheet and photo format that works
6. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

keyTakeaways: Most ID card delays come from photos and data, not printing.
One spreadsheet with one row per person and photos named by roll number prevents most errors.
IDGen Studio lets students or staff submit photos and details online; exact features depend on your account setup.
In India, student and staff data is personal data. Check the current DPDP Act and rules for what applies to your institution.

content.lead: Every year the same scene repeats in schools and colleges. Class teachers collect photos in envelopes, someone forwards fifty pictures over WhatsApp, names are spelt two ways, and a photo meant for roll 17 is saved as roll 71. Then the cards are printed, and the mistakes are on plastic. This guide explains how to collect the data properly, whether you use a spreadsheet or an online tool.

sections.heading: 1. Where ID card orders actually get stuck
body: In our experience, the time between the decision to order and the cards arriving is mostly spent on the data. Common causes are photos in different sizes and lighting, cropped heads, a missing class or section, names written in capitals in one place and lower case in another, and files renamed by hand.

A single misnamed photo shifts a person to the wrong card. Since the card has the photo, the name and the number together, any one error means a reprint of that card, and a wrong card in someone's hand.

sections.heading: 2. The spreadsheet and photo format that works
body: Whether you send the data to us or to anyone else, agree this format first.

• One spreadsheet, one row per person. Columns for name, class and section (or department and designation), roll or employee number, date of birth if required, guardian contact, and blood group if you want it printed.
• Names written once, in the form you want printed. Decide on capitals or title case and apply it to every row.
• One photo per person, named by roll or employee number, for example 1042.jpg, so that the file name is the link to the row.
• Photos taken against a plain light background, face straight on, in good light, at a reasonable resolution. A phone photo is fine if it is sharp and the face fills enough of the frame.
• A sample first. Send ten rows and ten photos before the full file so problems show up early.

tipBox.title: Name photos by number, never by name
tipBox.text: Names are spelt differently and repeated; numbers are unique. A photo named 1042.jpg can only belong to one row.

sections.heading: 3. Collecting online with IDGen Studio
body: If you do not want to chase photos by hand, IDGen Studio is IDGen's digital data-collection workflow. The idea is simple: each class, department or batch receives a link or QR code, and students or staff open it on their phones, check their details and upload a photo. The records reach the print queue in one structured file instead of a pile of messages.

What the portal does for a particular order, such as automatic cropping, background clean-up, approval steps or integration with your records, depends on your account setup, so ask the team which features apply to your order before relying on them.
Whatever tool you use, the principles are the same: one place for data, one version of each record, and a person responsible for approving each batch.

sections.heading: 4. Proof and sign-off
body: Before printing, ask for a proof. A proof is the one step that catches errors people no longer see, like a transposed digit in a roll number or a photo that is a slightly different person's.

Have two people check the proof against the source list: a teacher or department head for names and classes, and an office or admin person for numbers. When both agree, approve in writing. At IDGen the process runs from requirement to data check, proof, approval, production, quality check and dispatch, and orders are dispatched within 72 hours of approval.

sections.heading: 5. Handling student data responsibly
body: Photos, names, dates of birth and guardian contacts are personal data, and for students the data usually concerns minors. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is now being implemented in phases: the DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025, with the main obligations coming into effect after a transition of about eighteen months, around mid-2027.

The Act treats anyone under 18 as a child and generally requires verifiable parental consent for processing a child's data, but commentary on the Rules notes that educational institutions are given specific exemptions for educational activities and the safety of children. Details and limits matter here, and the commentary differs, so read the current Rules or ask a lawyer what applies to your institution.

Whatever the law says, sensible practice is straightforward: collect only what the card needs, share it only with the people making the card, keep it out of open WhatsApp groups where possible, and delete or return files when the job is done. IDGen treats customer data as confidential project information and uses it only for the printing you authorise.

sections.heading: 6. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
body: These are the mistakes we see most often.
• Collecting photos in a WhatsApp group where files are compressed and names are lost.
• Letting each class teacher choose their own format.
• Not agreeing the name spelling and case before collecting.
• Sending the full file without a ten-row test.
• Keeping student data open to anyone in the office after the job is done.

sections.heading: 7. Frequently asked questions
body: Do we need IDGen Studio to order cards? No. You can send a spreadsheet and photos. Studio is an option for collecting data online.
How should photos be named? By roll or employee number, for example 1042.jpg, so each file maps to one row.
What photo quality is enough? A sharp, straight-on face with a plain light background. Reject blurred or tilted photos at the source.
Who approves the data? Ideally a teacher or department head for names and classes, and an office person for numbers, both on the proof.
Is student data confidential with IDGen? IDGen treats customer data as confidential project information and uses it only for the authorised printing scope.

sources.title: Outlook Business: Govt notifies DPDP Rules, 2025
S.S. Rana & Co.: Schools and coaching centres processing children's data

title: Event Badges That Work: A Planning Guide for Conferences, Fests and Summits
seoTitle: Event Badge Planning Guide: Design, Lanyards, Printing
subtitle: Badge size, name legibility, colour coding, lanyards, on-site reprints and a timeline, drawn from how event teams actually run registration.
excerpt: Plan event badges properly: what to print, how large the name should be, colour coding, lanyard choices, QR or RFID, a reprint desk and a realistic timeline.
alt: Large format summit event badge with dual hook lanyard

tableOfContents.title: 1. Decide what the badge must do
2. Layout: name first, everything else second
5. On the day: reprints and spares
7. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

keyTakeaways: A badge has three jobs: tell people who someone is, show what they are allowed to do, and be easy to replace.
Print the first name large enough to read from a conversational distance; everything else is secondary.
Use at most four or five colours, and make each mean one thing.
Order spares, and plan a reprint desk.

content.lead: Event badges are noticed only when they fail: a name too small to read, a lanyard that flips the badge backwards, a VIP who is wearing the wrong colour at the wrong door. Most of these problems are cheap to prevent, and all of them are decided before a single badge is printed. This guide covers the decisions in the order we would make them.

sections.heading: 1. Decide what the badge must do
body: Write down the badge's jobs. For most events these are: identify the person (name and organisation), show their category (delegate, speaker, volunteer, press, VIP), grant or block access to certain areas or meals, and, for some events, record attendance through a QR code or RFID chip.

Each job has a design consequence. If the badge needs to be scanned, it needs a clear code and a flat, rigid surface. If it controls access, it needs a colour or symbol that a volunteer can read in a second.

sections.heading: 2. Layout: name first, everything else second
body: The name is the point. People read badges while standing a metre or two away, usually while talking, so the first name should be the largest text on the badge, with the organisation and category below it. Put the event name and logo smaller at the top or bottom, not in the middle.

Choose a plain, bold typeface. Avoid thin or decorative fonts and avoid text over busy backgrounds. Check long names early: if a name will not fit, decide in advance whether to shrink it or abbreviate it, rather than having the printer decide.
Keep the back useful. A programme, a Wi-Fi code, an emergency number or a venue map on the back turns a badge into something people keep wearing.

sections.heading: 3. Colour coding and access zones
body: Colour is the fastest signal. Use a colour band or a different lanyard colour per category, and keep it to four or five. When there are more categories than colours, use a short code or icon in addition.

Make each colour mean one thing across the whole event. If green is for volunteers at registration, do not also use green for a meal pass. Brief volunteers and security with a one-page key, and print the key on the back of the volunteer badges.

tipBox.title: Test in poor light
tipBox.text: Print one sample of each colour and look at it in the dimmest room and the brightest corridor of the venue. Colours that are clear on screen can look identical under stage lighting.

sections.heading: 4. Lanyards, holders and attachments
body: Width. A 20 mm lanyard is a common choice for adults and gives room for a printed logo or sponsor name. Sponsors often pay for lanyards, so decide early who gets the print area.
Material. Polyester ribbons suit full-colour sublimation printing. Satin has a smoother look.
Attachment. A fish hook or swivel hook is quick to attach and to change. Breakaway connectors release under a strong pull and are sensible where crowds, machinery or children are involved.
Holder. Choose a holder that matches your badge orientation, and one that lets the badge be changed on the day. Our holder guide explains the options.
Check that the badge hangs the right way up. A flipped badge hides the name, and the cure is usually a holder that does not rotate or a lanyard with a clip at the right position.

sections.heading: 5. On the day: reprints and spares
body: Expect late registrations, misspelt names and lost badges. Order spare blank badges in each category, in the same print run so the colours match, and set up a small reprint desk with a printer and the master list.
Hand out badges in alphabetical or category queues, with the list printed and a second copy on a laptop. If you use scanning, test the scanners on the real badges the evening before.

sections.heading: 6. A realistic timeline
body: Work backwards from the day.
• Four weeks before: settle categories, colours, layout and quantity.
• Three weeks before: send the artwork and the first data file. Approve a proof.
• Two weeks before: send the final list of names. Approve the final proof.
• Ten days before: production. At IDGen, orders are dispatched within 72 hours of approval, from our Guwahati facility, by courier.
• One week before: badges and lanyards arrive; check counts, test scanners, brief the registration team.
Late changes will always arrive. Keep ten to fifteen per cent spares and a reprint option rather than reopening the main order.

sections.heading: 7. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
body: These are the mistakes we see most often.
• Setting the name too small because the sponsor logo is large.
• Using more than five colours, so nobody remembers what each one means.
• Printing every badge only once, with no spares and no reprint option.
• Choosing a lanyard clip that flips the badge backwards.
• Testing scanners only on screen, not on the printed badge.

sections.heading: 8. Frequently asked questions
body: How many spares should we order? Ten to fifteen per cent is a sensible start for most events, split across categories.
What size should the name be? Large enough to read from a metre or two away; make it the largest text on the badge.
Can badges be both printed and scanned? Yes. Add a QR code or an RFID chip, and test the scanners on the real badges beforehand.
How early should we order? Four weeks before the event is comfortable for a first order; settle design and colours early.
Can sponsors get a lanyard print area? Yes, but agree the print area, text and colours early so the design is approved in time.

title: Ordering School ID Cards: A Checklist Before You Ask for a Quote
seoTitle: School ID Card Order Checklist: What to Prepare Before a Quote
subtitle: Everything a school or college office should have ready before ordering ID cards, so that the quote is accurate and the order is not delayed.
excerpt: A step-by-step checklist for schools and colleges ordering ID cards: card design, data and photos, accessories, deadlines, proofs and delivery planning.

tableOfContents.title: 5. What to send for a quote
7. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

keyTakeaways: List your groups first: students, teachers, non-teaching staff, drivers, visitors.
Fix your card design before collecting data; changing the design later restarts the checks.
Count spares: new admissions and replacements will come.
Order early; allow for proof, production, dispatch and courier time.

content.lead: A good quote needs a few facts, and a good order needs a few more. Schools that prepare these in advance get quotes the same day and cards well before the session starts. Here is the checklist we would work through if we were in your office.

sections.heading: 1. Decide who needs which card
body: Start with a list of groups. Most schools need cards for students, teachers, non-teaching staff and bus or van staff. Some also need visitor, parent pick-up or contractor cards.

For each group, decide the card design (a different colour band is enough), the lanyard colour and whether the group needs RFID. A card for a parent who picks up a child is different from a card for a teacher who marks attendance.

sections.heading: 2. Design decisions
body: Settle the layout before you collect data. Choose vertical or horizontal; our guide to card holders explains why that matters. Decide what appears on the front (photo, name, class and section, roll number, house, school logo) and on the back (address, emergency contact, bus route, blood group if you want it, return instructions).
Prepare your logo as a high-resolution file, preferably a vector file. Low-resolution logos copied from a website look blurred when printed.
Choose single-sided or double-sided printing. Double-sided costs more but gives you room for the back-of-card information.

sections.heading: 3. Data and photos
body: Use one spreadsheet with one row per person, and photos named by roll number. Decide the spelling and case for names and apply it throughout. Our guide on collecting student data explains the format in detail, and IDGen Studio can collect photos and details online if you prefer.
Check photos before sending: a clear face, a plain light background, no cropped heads, and a consistent look. Reject blurred or tilted photos at the source.
Send ten rows first as a test. It catches format problems while they are cheap to fix.

sections.heading: 4. Lanyards, holders and hooks
body: Decide whether you want only cards, cards with lanyards, or a full set with holders and hooks. A full set is the most convenient and the least likely to lose cards; our holder guide explains V-1, H-1 and V-2.
Choose the lanyard width and colour, and whether it carries the school name. Choose a hook type and whether a breakaway is needed for labs, sports or younger children.
Order spares: a few holders, lanyards and blank cards for new admissions.

sections.heading: 5. What to send for a quote
body: • School name and city.
• Quantity per group (students, teachers, staff, others).
• Card type: plain PVC or RFID, single or double sided.
• Accessories: lanyard width and print, holder model, hook type.
• Your logo file and any design you already have.
• A target date for the cards to be in your hands.
Use the quote form on the website, or WhatsApp the details. We reply with a price and the data format we need.

sections.heading: 6. Timing and delivery
body: Work back from the date you need the cards. Allow time for the quote and decisions, collecting and checking the data, the proof and its approval, production, and courier shipping.

At IDGen, an order is dispatched within 72 hours of approval from our facility in Guwahati and shipped by courier. Courier time depends on the route, so for towns far from Guwahati allow more. As a rule of thumb, start two to three weeks before you need the cards for a standard order, and earlier for large batches or for the start of a session.

sections.heading: 7. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
body: These are the mistakes we see most often.
• Collecting data before the card design is final.
• Forgetting transport and non-teaching staff when counting quantities.
• Sending a low-resolution logo copied from a web page.
• Not ordering spares for new admissions.
• Starting too late for the start of the session.

sections.heading: 8. Frequently asked questions
body: What is the minimum order? Small orders are possible, though per-card cost is higher on small runs. Ask for a quote on your quantity.
Do you need all the data at once? No. Send a ten-row test first, then the full file once the format is confirmed.
Can we use our existing design? Yes. Send the artwork and we will prepare a proof.
What if names are in more than one language? Share the exact wording at the proof stage so the layout can be checked.
How soon can we get the cards? Orders are dispatched within 72 hours of approval, plus courier time. Plan two to three weeks for a standard order.

title: Ordering ID Cards in Northeast India: Timelines, Shipping and Planning
seoTitle: Ordering ID Cards in Northeast India: Timeline and Shipping
subtitle: How an order moves from your request to your door when the production facility is in Guwahati and you are in Jorhat, Shillong, Kohima, Imphal or beyond.
excerpt: A practical guide to ordering ID cards from Guwahati for institutions across Assam and the Northeast: the steps, the timeline and how to plan around courier time.

tableOfContents.title: 1. How ordering works across the region
6. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

keyTakeaways: Production is in Guwahati; everything else, such as proofs, data and approvals, happens online.
Orders are dispatched within 72 hours of approval; courier time is extra and depends on the route.
Hill districts and the north bank can take longer; plan a margin.
Ask for a sample on large or first-time orders.

content.lead: Many of our customers are in towns where no ID card manufacturer has an office: Dhemaji, Tura, Jowai, Kohima, Aizawl, Agartala. That does not need to slow an order down, but it does mean planning differently from a customer in Guwahati. This is how an order works, step by step, and where the time goes.

sections.heading: 1. How ordering works across the region
body: IDGen produces cards at its facility in Guwahati and ships to customers across Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura and Sikkim by courier. We do not have local offices in those cities, and pages on this site that list a city describe service coverage rather than a branch.
In practice, you deal with us online and by phone. You send the requirement and data, review a proof, approve it, and receive the cards by courier.

sections.heading: 2. The steps in order
body: 1. Requirement: tell us the organisation, card type, quantity and accessories.
2. Quote: we send a price and the data format we need.
3. Data: you send the spreadsheet and photos, or collect them through IDGen Studio.
4. Proof: we send a digital proof, or a physical pre-production sample for larger projects where available.
5. Approval: you approve in writing.
6. Production and quality check: cards are printed, checked, and prepared for dispatch.
7. Dispatch: orders leave Guwahati within 72 hours of approval and are handed to a courier.
8. Delivery: the courier delivers to your address; tracking depends on the courier.

sections.heading: 3. Courier time and planning
body: The 72 hours is the time from your approval to dispatch from Guwahati. It does not include courier time. Courier time depends on the destination and the carrier, and we do not promise a fixed number of days.

Plan backwards. Take the date you need the cards, subtract courier time with a margin, subtract three days for dispatch, subtract the time you need for data checks and approval, and that is the date to send your requirement. For most institutions in Assam, two to three weeks before the date is comfortable; for hill districts and far corners, add more.

tipBox.title: Add a margin, not a hope
tipBox.text: If the cards are needed for an event or the first day of a session, aim to have them a week early. A delay in transit then becomes an inconvenience, not a crisis.

sections.heading: 4. Smaller towns and hill districts
body: North-bank districts such as Dhemaji and Lakhimpur, and hill towns in Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Sikkim, are reached by longer courier routes, and the monsoon can affect them. We recommend ordering earlier for these destinations and giving us a full delivery address with a phone number, since couriers often call before delivering.
If several institutions in one town are ordering, ask us whether the orders can be shipped together; it can reduce the number of parcels.

sections.heading: 5. Samples and reorders
body: For a first order, or a large batch, ask for a physical pre-production sample. It lets you check colours, the card feel, the holder and the lanyard in hand. We confirm what is available for your order.
For a reorder, your approved design can be reused, so you send only the new data. Tell us which previous order you want to repeat and what has changed.

sections.heading: 6. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
body: These are the mistakes we see most often.
• Counting from the quote date, not the approval date, when planning delivery.
• Giving an incomplete delivery address, so the courier cannot reach you.
• Ordering for a hard deadline with no margin.
• Not telling us the reader model for RFID cards until after approval.
• Assuming a city page on the website means a local office.

sections.heading: 7. Frequently asked questions
body: Do you have a local office in my city? No. We produce in Guwahati and serve the region by courier, with proofs and data handled online.
How long does delivery take? We dispatch within 72 hours of approval; courier time depends on the destination and carrier.
Can you ship to towns outside the cities? Yes. Give us the full address and a phone number.
Can I track my order? Tracking depends on the courier.
Can I see a sample first? Ask for a physical pre-production sample on a first or large order; we will confirm what is available.
